newsitem.title: KENYA: FOCUS-Kenya shilling slumps after IMF aid ruling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kenya shilling slumps after IMF aid ruling.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling slumped on Friday after news that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had halted its lending programme amid mounting concern that the government was not doing enough to crack down on corruption.
"The Kenyan shilling opened at 59/59.50 versus the dollar and then depreciated to 60/62.50 within 20 minutes," a dealer at Barclays Bank of Kenya told Reuters.
There were bids at as low as 64.50 for two leading commercial banks. But many banks were tied in the 60 to 63 band versus the dollar compared to around 59 at close on Thursday.
Kenyan Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said in a statement that the government would let market forces determine shilling direction but it still hoped to maintain price stability.
Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem said the bank was weighing the market and would not "join in a stampede".

The foreign exchange dealers said trading was at its most nervous in Kenya since October 1993 when the shilling fell to a record low 69 versus the dollar and around 130 against the pound at the height of economic mismanagement, dealers said.

"Spreads are still very wide. The market is very nervous. We've seen a lot of demand at levels above 60 and 61 buying," a commercial bank dealer told Reuters. Some commercial banks posted bid orders of as low as 64.50 against the dollar.
Other commercial dealers said they were receiving buy orders from offshore clients -- ranging between $1.5-$4 million.
"The central bank has not yet come in either directly or through any commercial bank," said Charles Musau, a senior dealer at the central bank.

The decision by the IMF was not unprecendented but came as a shock. The Kenyan government has implemented economic reform measures since 1993 and the IMF was thought to have confidence in the management style and ability of Cheserem and Mudavadi.
But political questions, including slow progress in constitutional reforms, had dampened business sentiment.
In November 1991, the IMF suspended balance of payments support to Kenya pending a switch to pluralist politics.

An IMF spokesman said a $205 million three-year loan, offered under the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility, would be allowed to lapse because the governemnt's response to a July 24 deadline had been inadequate.
News that the IMF is not extending the loan is bound to alarm already-nervous Kenyan markets and have negative implications on other bilateral programmes of loans and aid.

"That is pretty sad. We had made strong gains in the field of economic reform in the last few years and that IMF decision will take us back two to three steps," said John Munge, managing director at leading brokerage house Shah, Munge & Partners.
Economic analysts said the benchmark for the shilling versus dollar rate would be 62 to 65 and up to 100 on the pound.
They said that the IMF decision had left Kenya with a turbulent exchange rate and it was uncertain whether the central bank would intervene massively to stem the shilling slide.
"The markets will move regardless of what the central bank does," a leading investment adviser told Reuters.

One senior dealer said that Kenya had survived without IMF aid for three years before -- in 1991 to 1993 -- and coping would not be a major problem. What worried markets was the initial panic that would follow the decision.
